options: A) Microorganism is a fundamental concept in The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye.

questions.question_text: State two ecological benefits of decomposers in nature.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: 1. They break down dead plant and animal matter, preventing waste accumulation. 2. They recycle essential inorganic nutrients back into soil and water for plant uptake.

questions.question_text: Explain why adding starter curd to extremely hot boiling milk fails to produce curd.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: Boiling milk temperature denatures the proteins and kills the live Lactobacillus bacteria present in the starter curd. Without active living bacteria, fermentation of lactose to lactic acid cannot occur.

sections.section_name: Section C (Long Answer & Case Study Questions)

questions.question_text: Discuss the major economic and industrial applications of microorganisms across agriculture, medicine, and food production.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: 1. Agriculture: Rhizobium bacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen in legume root nodules to enrich soil fertility. 2. Medicine: Fungi like Penicillium produce life-saving antibiotics; weakened pathogens are used to prepare vaccines. 3. Food Industry: Lactobacillus ferments milk into curd/cheese; yeast produces CO2 to make bread soft and fluffy. 4. Waste & Energy: Methanogenic bacteria break down organic waste to produce biogas fuel and rich manure.

questions.question_text: Explain how decomposers maintain ecological balance.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: Decomposers break down dead plant and animal matter into simple inorganic compounds. This recycles essential nutrients back into soil and water, preventing organic waste accumulation.

questions.question_text: Explain the principle of 2.2 Classification and Ecological Significance of Microorganisms and state its scientific significance.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: Microbes fall into 5 primary groups: Bacteria (prokaryotic, unicellular), Microalgae (photosynthetic, produces >50% Earth O2), Fungi (decomposers, yeast), Protozoa (unicellular eukaryotes like Amoeba), and Viruses (acellular obligate intracellular parasites). [Think like a scientist: Are Viruses Living?] Viruses remain inert crystals outside living hosts, exhibiting life characteristics only after entering host cells.

questions.question_text: Explain the principle of 2.1 Unveiling the Microscopic World and Optical Tools and state its scientific significance.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: Human vision cannot resolve objects smaller than ~0.1 mm. Lenses bend light rays to magnify microscopic structures. Robert Hooke observed cork cells (1665), and Leeuwenhoek observed free-living 'animacules' (bacteria/protozoa). The foldscope provides low-cost field magnification up to 140x. [Heritage Note: Ancient Indian Concept of Krimi] Vedic texts classified tiny living entities as 'Krimi', categorizing them into Drishya (macro/visible) and Adrishya (micro/invisible).

questions.question_text: Explain the principle of 2.2 Classification and Ecological Significance of Microorganisms and state its scientific significance.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: Microbes fall into 5 primary groups: Bacteria (prokaryotic, unicellular), Microalgae (photosynthetic, produces >50% Earth O2), Fungi (decomposers, yeast), Protozoa (unicellular eukaryotes like Amoeba), and Viruses (acellular obligate intracellular parasites). [Think like a scientist: Are Viruses Living?] Viruses remain inert crystals outside living hosts, exhibiting life characteristics only after entering host cells.
